{{Short description|Mathematical theorem}}
In [[real analysis]], a branch of [[mathematics]], '''Bernstein's theorem''', named after [[Sergei Bernstein]], states that every [[real number|real]]-valued [[function (mathematics)|function]] on the half-line {{closed-open|0, ∞}} that is '''[[Completely monotone function|completely monotone]]''' is a mixture of [[exponential function]]s or in more abstract language, that it is the [[Laplace transform]] of a positive [[Borel measure]] on {{closed-open|0, ∞}}.  In one important special case the mixture is a [[weighted average]], or [[expected value]].  It is also known as the '''Bernstein–Widder theorem''' or '''Hausdorff–Bernstein–Widder theorem'''.

== History ==
The result was first proved by Bernstein in 1928,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bernstein|first=Serge|date=1929|title=Sur les fonctions absolument monotones|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.acta/1485887795|journal=Acta Mathematica|language=en|volume=52|issue=0|pages=1–66|doi=10.1007/BF02592679|issn=0001-5962|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and similar results were discussed by [[David Widder]] in 1931<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Widder|first=D. V.|date=1931|title=Necessary and Sufficient Conditions for the Representation of a Function as a Laplace Integral|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1989513?origin=crossref|journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society|volume=33|issue=4|pages=851|doi=10.2307/1989513}}</ref> who refers to Bernstein but states that "The author had completed the proof of this theorem a few months after the publication of Bernstein's paper without being aware of its existence".  The most cited reference is the 1941 book by Widder called The Laplace Transform.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Widder|first=David Vernon|url=https://www.google.fr/books/edition/The_Laplace_Transform/cDAPAAAAIAAJ|title=The Laplace Transform|date=1941|publisher=Princeton University Press|language=en|doi=10.2307/3605681}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Widder|first=David Vernon|title=The Laplace Transform (PMS-6)|date=2016|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-1-4008-7645-7|series=Princeton Mathematical Series|location=Princeton, NJ}}</ref> Later a simpler proof<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://m.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=rm&paperid=6870&what=fullt&option_lang=eng|title=On two theorems from the theory of absolutely monotonic functions|last=Korenblum|first=Boris|date=1951|journal=Uspekhi Matematicheskikh Nauk|issue=4|volume=6|pages=172–175}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Totally Monotone Functions with Applications to the Bergman Space|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2154243?origin=crossref|journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society|date=1993|pages=795|volume=337|issue=2|doi=10.2307/2154243|first=B.|last=Korenblum|first2=R.|last2=O'Neil|first3=K.|last3=Richards|first4=K.|last4=Zhu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://djalil.chafai.net/blog/2013/03/23/the-bernstein-theorem-on-completely-monotone-functions/|title=The Bernstein theorem on completely monotone functions|date=2013-03-23|last=Chafaï|first=Djalil}}</ref> was given by [[Boris Korenblum]].  At around the same time [[Gustave Choquet]] studied the much more general concept of monotone functions on [[semigroup]]s and gave a more abstract proof<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Theory of capacities|url=https://aif.centre-mersenne.org/articles/10.5802/aif.53/|journal=Annales de l'Institut Fourier|date=1954|issn=1777-5310|pages=131–295|volume=5|doi=10.5802/aif.53|language=en|first=Gustave|last=Choquet}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|edition=2nd|title=Lectures on Choquet's theorem|publisher=Springer|date=2001|location=Berlin; New York|isbn=978-3-540-41834-4|series=Lecture notes in mathematics|first=Robert R.|last=Phelps}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://yelmaazouz.org/content/documents/Choquet_Theorem.pdf|title=On Choquet's Theorem|last=El Maazouz|first=Yassine}}</ref><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|title=New characterizations of completely monotone functions and Bernstein functions, a converse to Hausdorff's moment characterization theorem|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1319516618300288|journal=Arab Journal of Mathematical Sciences|date=2019|pages=57–82|volume=25|issue=1|doi=10.1016/j.ajmsc.2018.03.001|language=en|first=Rafik|last=Aguech|first2=Wissem|last2=Jedidi|doi-access=free}}</ref> based on the [[Krein–Milman theorem]].  [[Felix Hausdorff]] had earlier characterised [[complete monotonicity|completely monotone sequence]]s. These are the sequences occurring in the [[Hausdorff moment problem]].

== Statement of the theorem ==
''Complete monotonicity'' of a function {{math|''f''}} means that {{math|''f''}} is [[continuous function|continuous]] on {{closed-open|0, ∞}}, [[infinitely differentiable]] on {{open-open|0, ∞}}, and satisfies<math display="block">(-1)^n \frac{d^n}{dt^n} f(t) \geq 0</math>for all nonnegative [[integer]]s {{mvar|n}} and for all {{math|''t'' > 0}}.

The "weighted average" statement can be characterized thus: there is a non-negative finite [[Borel measure]] on {{closed-open|0, ∞}} with [[cumulative distribution function]] {{math|''g''}} such that<math display="block">f(t) = \int_0^\infty e^{-tx} \, dg(x),</math>the [[integral]] being a [[Riemann–Stieltjes integral]].

== Bernstein functions ==
Nonnegative functions whose [[derivative]] is completely monotone are called ''Bernstein functions''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Schilling |first=René L. |title=Bernstein Functions: Theory and Applications |date=2010 |publisher=Walter de Gruyter GmbH |others=Renming Song, Zoran Vondraček |isbn=978-3-11-021531-1 |series=De Gruyter Studies in Mathematics |location=Berlin/Boston}}</ref>  Every Bernstein function has the [[Lévy–Khintchine representation]]:<math display="block">f(t) = a + bt + \int_0^\infty \left(1 - e^{-tx}\right) \mu(dx),</math>where <math>a,b \geq 0</math> and <math>\mu</math> is a measure on the positive real half-line such that<math display="block">\int_0^\infty \left(1\wedge x\right) \mu(dx) < \infty.</math>

== Schoenberg–Williamson theorem ==
The Schoenberg–Williamson theorem (also called Schoenberg's theorem on multiply monotone functions, Williamson's representation theorem) is the finite-order version of Bernstein's theorem.  A k-monotone (or k-times monotone) function satisfies<math display="block">(-1)^n \frac{d^n}{dt^n} f(t) \geq 0 \quad\text{for}\,\, \, 0 \leq n \leq k</math>The Schoenberg–Williamson theorem says that f is k-monotone on {{Open-open|0, ∞}} if and only if<math display="block">f(t)=\int_0^\infty (x-t)_+^{k-1} \, d\mu(x)</math>for some positive measure <math>\mu</math> on {{Open-open|0, ∞}}.

The proof was published by Williamson in 1956<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Williamson |first=R. E. |date=1956-06-01 |title=Multiply monotone functions and their Laplace transforms |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/duke-mathematical-journal/volume-23/issue-2/Multiply-monotone-functions-and-their-Laplace-transforms/10.1215/S0012-7094-56-02317-1.full |journal=Duke Mathematical Journal |volume=23 |issue=2 |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-56-02317-1 |issn=0012-7094|url-access=subscription }}</ref> but in his paper he mentions that "This formula was discovered by Schoenberg in 1940 but has remained unpublished".

Using the Taylor series of <math>f</math> with integral remainder, a more precise formula can be given<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Mattner |first=Lutz |date=1993 |title=Bernstein's theorem, inversion formula of Post and Widder, and the uniqueness theorem for Laplace transforms |url=https://www.math.uni-trier.de/~mattner/Mattner_1993_Bernstein_theorem_etc.pdf |journal=Expositiones Mathematicae |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=137–140}}</ref><math display="block">f(t) = \int_0^\infty \left(1-\frac{tx}{n}\right)_+^{n-1} f_n(x) \, dx</math>with<math display="block">f_n(x) = \frac{(-1)^n}{n!} \left(\frac{n}{x}\right)^{n+1} f^{(n)} \left(\frac{n}{x}\right) I(x>0)</math>where <math>f^{(n)}(t) = \frac{d^n}{dt^n} f(t)</math> and <math>I(x>0)</math> is the indicator function of <math>\mathbb{R}_+^*</math>.

Note then that if <math>f</math> is completely monotone then it is k-monotone for all <math>k \in \mathbb{N}</math> and the [[Post inversion formula|Post–Widder inversion formula]] states that <math>f_n</math>converge in distribution to <math>\mu</math> and <math>\left(1-\frac{tx}{n}\right)_+^{n-1}</math> converges to <math>e^{-tx}</math>as <math>n</math> goes to infinity, and we recover Bernstein's theorem.<ref name=":0" />
